title: Question 8.3
statement_text: For which sets $\mathcal{S}$ of strings is it true that there is a constant $c=c(\mathcal{S})\in\mathbb{N}$ such that every $c$-padded string $S$ contains either a string in $\mathcal{S}$ or the reverse of a string in $\mathcal{S}$ as a consecutive substring?
context_text: Strings are binary (over $\{0,1\}$). For $c\in\mathbb{N}$, a string is $c$-padded if it starts and ends with at least $c$ zeroes but is not the all-zero string. Graph motivation: a strand is a graph obtained from a path $P$ by adding a vertex $x$ (the neck) with at least one neighbour in $P$; it is a $c$-strand if $x$ is not adjacent to the first and last $c$ vertices of $P$. A $c$-tassel is obtained from at least $c$ disjoint copies of a $c$-strand by identifying their necks. A family $\mathcal{H}$ is tasselled if there is $c$ such that every $c$-tassel contains (as induced subgraphs) all components of some $H\in\mathcal{H}$. The paper proves that for finite $\mathcal{H}$, the class of $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs is clean (its only induced-subgraph obstructions to bounded treewidth are the basic ones: large cliques, complete bipartite graphs, subdivided walls and their line graphs) if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ is tasselled. A strand with neck $v$ and path $p_1\dots p_t$ is encoded by the string $S_{P,v}=b_1\dots b_t$ with $b_i=1$ iff $p_i$ is adjacent to $v$ (unique up to reversal); strands of a $c$-tassel give exactly the $c$-padded strings. When every graph of $\mathcal{H}$ is itself a tassel, deciding whether $\mathcal{H}$ is tasselled amounts to this question about the set $\mathcal{S}$ of their strings. A set $\mathcal{S}$ with the property is called a $c$-unavoidable language. The only singleton $c$-unavoidable languages are $\{0\cdots01\}$ (up to reversal) and $\{0\cdots0\}$, while larger ones seem hard to describe (e.g. $\{00011, 0001000, 1010, 010010, 111, 110011, 11011, 110010011, 00010011001000\}$ is 3-unavoidable); for finite $\mathcal{S}$ the property is decidable by a finite test. Unlike the classical unavoidable languages, whose minimal members are finite, minimal $c$-unavoidable languages may be infinite: $\{01^k0:k\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is 1-unavoidable but no proper subset is.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XIII. Basic obstructions in $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs for finite $\mathcal{H}$

title: Question 8.4
statement_text: For which sets $\mathcal{S}$ of strings is it true that every sufficiently long string contains a string in $\mathcal{S}$ as a consecutive substring?
context_text: These sets $\mathcal{S}$ are the classical unavoidable languages; it is known (from [4,5]) that every minimal unavoidable language is finite. This finiteness fails for $c$-unavoidable languages (e.g., $\mathcal{S}=\{01^{k}0:k\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is $1$-unavoidable), and the paper poses the question of which results on unavoidable languages generalise to the $c$-unavoidable setting introduced in Question 8.3.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XIII. Basic obstructions in $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs for finite $\mathcal{H}$
